b: The latest from Mari Rubio builds complex scaffolding from the simplest of motifs

Over the last few years, I’ve seen More Eaze (aka Mari Rubio) twice. At Rewire in 2022, she performed as —–__, a digital, detail-laden project created in collaboration with Seth Graham. Three years later, at the Supersonic Festival, I saw her with Water Damage. They played a single suite lasting almost fifty minutes. Rubio contributed long, bourdon violin parts, whilst the whole band stubbornly stuck to a motif that might just as easily have lasted ten minutes or several hours. Not much seemed to be happening, but the music kept shifting: the proportions, tension and weight of the sound changed, though the figure underpinning it remained virtually untouched.

I find myself thinking of that concert whilst listening to Valley and Structure, More Eaze’s second solo album released this year. The repetition here ceases to be a means of achieving a trance or a sense of monumentality. What happens to sound when we don’t let it go?

This question suits an artist who ranges from drone violin and ambient to electroacoustics, noise, auto-tune, and distorted pop. Rubio has recorded with Claire Rousay, Wendy Eisenberg and Tasha, and collaborated with Faye Webster and Chanel Beads. She grew up in Texas, playing the guitar and violin, performing at open mics and with local country songwriters. Folk is a natural idiom for her – one she can return to after many years, discovering she still remembers its syntax, even though she now speaks quite differently.

She did this most directly on Sentence Structure In The Country album, released in March. It was a peculiar kind of Americana record where pedal steel and folk melodies met auto-tune, post-rock stretching and minimalism. One of the album’s most interesting aspects was the tension between technology and what is traditionally considered the ‘authentic’ sound of American roots music. Rubio’s voice trembled, cracked and shifted in pitch thanks to auto-tune, yet this electronic mediation did not rob it of its intimacy. The processing became a means of revealing it: country ceased to signify a set of recognisable gestures. What remained was their memory.

Valley and Structure perform a similar operation, except that its subject is no longer the genre, but composition itself. Even the word ‘structure’, recurring in the titles of individual tracks, sounds like a command. Rubio does not use the ostinato as a scaffold upon which to build the actual composition. It is the ostinato itself that is the composition.

At first, something like Steve Reich emerges. Tiny, discrete elements form a system and the ear begins to pick up on the slightest shifts between them. But the repetitions are more fragile, momentarily taking on the lightness of a folk melody, then thickening until they become almost dramatic, and subsequently revealing the space around them once more. It reminds me of early albums by Jim O’Rourke or Sam Prekop: that lightness of music constructed with great precision, which nevertheless does not sound like a demonstration of the system. But also of Sarah Hennies, particularly her monumental The Reinvention of Romance.

Both artists share the conviction that a very simple idea can be stretched so long that it reveals possibilities that were initially impossible to hear within it. The individual figures are almost absurdly stable, so the slightest change in their surroundings becomes an event. A new harmony can alter the meaning of a motif repeated for several minutes. The voice’s appearance makes the abstract structure resemble a song for a moment. A moment later, the voice disappears, or the structure shifts beneath it, and the song ceases to exist once more. Something childlike also comes through here. The ostinato is one of the most elementary musical pleasures: playing something we like and then playing it again to see if we like it just as much the second time round. Rubio’s repetitions retain something of that primal curiosity.

It is hard not to see ‘Once You Say Yes To The Structure, You Never Get Out’, the title of the album’s twenty-minute centrepiece, as the motto for the whole record. Interestingly, once Rubio has indeed ‘stuck with it’, the music begins to feel increasingly free-flowing. Valley and Structure ask how little needs to be done for a structure to come to life. Rubio finds a motif and sticks with it. She does not try to overcome it or steer it towards a resolution but lets it persist long enough for it to change – not so much in the sound itself as in the way we hear it.
